🥇 Sequestering Jerusalem's Gold — why old coins needed a special verse

overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Arithmetic of Redemption Money
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 50a–50b
overview.hebrewSource: אָמַר רָבָא: סִילְעִים דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא תְּלָתָא וְתִילְתָּא הָוֵי
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Having established that five sela of Tyrian coinage redeem a firstborn, the Gemara now works out the practical exchange rate against dinars in circulation, including worn Roman coins from Hadrian and Trajan. Rava argues the Torah's sela is actually three and a third dinars, not four, based on the twenty gera of a shekel — a claim tested against a baraita about redeeming a consecrated field. The daf then explores why old coinage bearing traces of Jerusalem's gold needed special scriptural permission to use, and closes with Rav Asi's broad rule distinguishing Torah-mandated payments (Tyrian coinage) from rabbinically set fines (provincial coinage), tested against betrothal, tithe, and consecrated property.

slides.title: 🧮 Rabbi Yoḥanan's Formula for Redemption Coins
slides.subtitle: Working out five sela from worn Hadrianic and Trajanic dinars

steps.content: 1️⃣ Take worn gold dinars of Hadrian and Trajan, sold at 25 dinars per unit
2️⃣ First attempt: deduct one-sixth — but the math comes out short (21 less 1/6)
3️⃣ Second attempt: deduct one-sixth and one more dinar — still imprecise
4️⃣ Final formula: first deduct one dinar (leaving 24), THEN deduct one-sixth of that — yields exactly the five sela needed for redemption

callout.label: Why so complicated:
callout.text: The Gemara works through several failed formulas before landing on the precise sequence, showing how carefully redemption value had to be calibrated.

slides.title: ⚖️ How Many Dinars Is a Torah Sela?
slides.subtitle: Rava's claim tested against a baraita on field redemption

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: The Torah's sela weighs three and a third dinars — the verse says 'the shekel is twenty gera,' translated as twenty ma'a, and six ma'a make a dinar.

lines.speaker: Challenge
lines.text: But a baraita on redeeming a Jubilee-year field counts 48 pundeyon per sela — that's 24 ma'a, not 20!

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: That baraita describes coinage AFTER the Sages added one-sixth (four ma'a) to every sela — the Torah's original value was still 20 ma'a.

lines.speaker: Support
lines.text: A baraita confirms: the verse 'twenty gera shall be the shekel' permits adding to the value, but never reducing it below twenty.

callout.label: Real-world echo:
callout.text: Rav Ashi sent 17 dinars for a redemption and asked for a third back; Rav Aḥa replied asking for three MORE dinars — each following a different accounting of the sela's value.

slides.title: 🥇 Sequestering the Gold and Silver of the World
slides.subtitle: Why worn coinage needed a special verse to remain usable
rows: Rabbi Oshaya: all gold/silver almost sequestered because of Jerusalem's Temple treasury
Is Jerusalem really 'the majority of the world'?
Abaye reframes: only the worn Hadrianic/Trajanic dinars were at risk, since they contained plundered Temple silver
Verse permitting use: 'Robbers shall enter and profane it' (Ezekiel 7:22)
Once gentiles plundered the Temple's treasures, they lost their sanctity
This applies specifically to the coins bearing traces of that plundered silver

slides.title: 🏛️ Tyrian Coinage vs. Provincial Coinage
slides.subtitle: Rav Asi's rule, and where it gets refined

boxes.title: Unspecified Torah Money
items: Rav Yehuda cites Rav Asi: 'silver' in the Torah = Tyrian dinars (high value)
Applies to firstborn redemption, the ox-slave, rapist, seducer, defamer

boxes.title: Rabbinic Money
items: Money in statements of the Sages = provincial coinage (roughly 1/8 the value)
Example: the fine for striking someone is a provincial sela = half a dinar

boxes.title: Refined Version
items: Challenges from betrothal, tithe, and consecrated property force a narrower rule
Final version: only a SET, specific Torah sum is Tyrian; general mentions can vary

slides.title: ❓ Testing Rav Asi's Rule Against Other Halakhot
slides.subtitle: Four objections and how each is resolved

nodes.content: ⚖️ Oath of partial admission needs 'two silver [coins]' — is that two Tyrian coins? No, it's derived from a juxtaposition to 'vessels,' not from Rav Asi's rule
🌾 Second tithe money can be copper, not just silver — the doubled word 'money, money' is an amplification allowing any coinage
🕊️ Consecrated property redeemed for a peruta's worth — derived by verbal analogy from tithe, not from Rav Asi's rule
💍 Betrothal follows Beit Hillel's peruta, not Beit Shammai's dinar — so the rule is restated: only a SET Torah sum is Tyrian coinage

summary.principle: Redemption's five sela has a precise, debated numerical value in circulating coinage, and the broader principle that Torah-mandated sums use Tyrian coinage while rabbinic sums use provincial coinage survives only in a narrowed form.

flowSteps.content: 🧮 Rabbi Yoḥanan's formula converts worn dinars into exactly five redemption sela
⚖️ Rava: Torah's sela = 3⅓ dinars originally; Sages later added a sixth, reaching 4 dinars

columns.content: 🥇 Worn coins needed a special verse due to plundered Temple silver mixed within them
🏛️ Rav Asi: Torah's SET sums use Tyrian coinage; rabbinic sums use provincial coinage

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: precision in coin value is essential — an underpayment does not fulfill the mitzva of redemption

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yoḥanan's final formula, how does one arrive at five redemption sela from worn Hadrianic/Trajanic dinars sold at 25 per unit?
o: Deduct one-sixth only
Deduct one dinar first, then one-sixth of the remaining 24
Deduct one-third
Add one dinar, then deduct one-sixth
quiz.e: After two imprecise attempts, the Gemara concludes: first deduct one dinar (leaving 24), then deduct one-sixth of that remainder, yielding exactly the correct value for five sela.

quiz.q: According to Rava, how many dinars did the Torah's original sela weigh?
o: Four dinars
Three and one-third dinars
Six dinars
Two dinars
quiz.e: Rava derives from 'the shekel is twenty gera' (translated as twenty ma'a) and the rule that six ma'a equal one dinar, that the Torah's sela equals three and one-third dinars — before the Sages later added one-sixth to reach four.

quiz.q: Why does the baraita about redeeming a Jubilee-year field count 48 pundeyon per sela, seemingly contradicting Rava's calculation of 20 ma'a per sela?
o: The baraita is discussing a different verse entirely
That baraita reflects coinage after the Sages added one-sixth to the sela's value
Pundeyon and ma'a are unrelated units
The baraita is simply incorrect
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that the baraita describes the sela's value after the Sages augmented it by one-sixth (four ma'a), whereas Rava's calculation reflects the Torah's original, unaugmented value of twenty ma'a.

quiz.q: Why did the Sages initially seek to sequester (hide away) all the worn Hadrianic and Trajanic dinars in circulation?
o: Because those coins were counterfeit
Because they contained silver and gold that had been plundered from the Jerusalem Temple treasury
Because Roman coins were always forbidden
Because they lacked a mint mark
quiz.e: Abaye explains the concern was that these particular worn coins contained gold and silver looted from the Temple treasury; a verse in Ezekiel (7:22) about robbers profaning the sacred wealth ultimately permitted their continued use.

quiz.q: According to Rav Yehuda citing Rav Asi (in its final, narrowed form), when does an unspecified sum of 'money' in the Torah refer to Tyrian coinage?
o: Every single mention of money anywhere in Tanakh
Only when the Torah sets a specific fixed amount, like the five sela of redemption
Only in cases involving betrothal
Never — it's always provincial coinage
quiz.e: After challenges from oath law, tithe, consecrated property, and betrothal, the rule is refined: only a Torah passage stating a SET, specific sum (like the five sela for redemption, or fifty shekels for a rapist) is understood as Tyrian coinage.
